user_reported.status: not recognized in the recording (it may be outside the clip, brief, or missed by the recognizer)

explained_behaviors.summary: Flicking, twitching or lashing the tail while the rest of the body may be still.
explained_behaviors.temporal_notes: A relaxed cat holds its tail up without flicking; the speed and context of the movement matter.

play_or_normal.explanation: attention to prey or a moving target (for example birds outside a window): a hunting cat watches with a twitching tail before it lunges

request.explanation: a signal that the cat wants contact to stop: during petting or handling, tail lashing or twitching often comes before a swat or bite

arousal_or_stress.explanation: irritation or arousal from something it cannot reach or does not like (an outdoor cat seen through a window, being disturbed while resting)

medical.explanation: with rippling skin over the back and sudden running, part of an episode of feline hyperaesthesia

uncertainty: The recording can show what the animal does and when; it cannot establish why. Candidate explanations come from the cited sources, ordered by how well your description matches them.
Behaviour recognition uses a general vision-language model (zero-shot); scores are relative, not probabilities, and its measured accuracy is in results/e31.
observations_needed: What is the cat looking at or reacting to while the tail moves?
Does it happen while it is being petted or handled, and does a swat or bite follow?
Does the skin on the back ripple at the same time?
urgent_signs: tail flicking with skin rippling, dilated pupils and sudden running or self-attack (possible hyperaesthesia episode)

sources.supports: a hunting cat slinks with a lowered head and a twitching tail and lunges when prey is in reach

sources.citation: Cornell Feline Health Center: Feline behavior problems: aggression.
sources.supports: petting-induced aggression (over-stimulation, the cat controlling when petting ends) is often preceded by dilated pupils, tail lashing and ears moved back; a relaxed cat holds its tail up with no flicking or twitching; seeing an outdoor cat through a window can trigger redirected aggression; cats in pain may act aggressively to avoid touch

sources.citation: Animal Humane Society: Petting-induced and play aggression in cats.
sources.supports: tail lashing or thumping, shifting body position, skin twitching and direct stares indicate the cat has had enough petting

sources.citation: Kim SA (2025) Behavior problems of cats. Merck Veterinary Manual.
sources.supports: petting-induced aggression from low tolerance of contact or over-stimulation; arousal can be redirected; some cats use threatening displays to remove a fear-evoking stimulus; medical problems must be ruled out before a problem is called behavioural

sources.citation: Cornell Feline Health Center: Hyperesthesia syndrome.
sources.supports: skin sensitivity near the base of the tail; scratching, biting, tail chasing, dilated pupils, rippling skin; underlying causes (for example disc disease) must be evaluated; stress adds to the reaction

sources.citation: Today's Veterinary Practice: Answering FAQs about feline hyperesthesia syndrome.
sources.supports: diagnosis of exclusion; consider skin disease and spinal, tail and anal-sac pain; consider focal seizures when episodes are stereotyped, abrupt and not interruptible; many signs also occur in healthy cats

answer.summary: No specific behaviour was recognized with confidence in the recording. Movement: its appearance repeats about every 1.8 s. Flicking, twitching or lashing the tail (user report only) has several possible explanations, in order of fit to your description: ordinary play or maintenance behaviour; a request or intention directed at a person; arousal, frustration or stress; discomfort, itch, pain or a neurological cause. The cause is not established from the recording; the questions listed would help tell the candidates apart.
